reason: Accretion releases heat, so combining it with the young Earth should begin the melting needed for differentiation.
expectation: Earth heats up and develops molten material.

effect: Accretion heat produced a magma ocean, providing molten material for differentiation.
reaction: The distinction between molten rock and the growing metal core is useful.
reason: Gravity should help dense metal separate from the molten silicate.
expectation: Dense metal sinks toward Earth’s core, separating from the silicate.

effect: Gravity was not a direct partner for the magma ocean; metal grains and convection are available instead.
reaction: The compatibility feedback clarifies the next step.
reason: Metal grains are the more direct choice for separating metal from silicate.
expectation: The metal will contribute to a denser region or growing core.

alternatives.reason: Convection may instead advance the crust-forming goal.

effect: The metal is now represented as droplets within the silicate melt, ready to separate under gravity.
reaction: The intermediate makes the separation process clearer.
reason: Gravity should draw the denser metal droplets downward through the melt.
expectation: The metal collects toward the centre, advancing core formation.

effect: Gravity caused the metal to sink and merge, advancing differentiation.
reaction: The multiple possible pathways make the simplified process clearer.
reason: I’ll check what can advance the sinking metal toward a differentiated interior.
expectation: The available partner should lead toward formation of Earth’s core.

effect: The sinking metal and magma ocean formed an iron-rich core beneath a silicate mantle, completing differentiation.
reaction: The distinction between ongoing separation and inserting a ready-made core is useful.
reason: Convection in molten silicate is the remaining known partner for the magma ocean and may advance crust formation.
expectation: Convection will change the molten silicate and help lead toward crustal rafts.

effect: Convection brought hot melt to the surface, where it can lose heat.
reaction: The connection between convection and surface cooling is clear.
reason: Radiation can carry heat away from the surface melt, allowing it to cool toward crust formation.
expectation: The surface melt cools and begins to solidify.

effect: Surface cooling produced crystals and a thin solid layer above hot rock.
reaction: The crystallization step clarifies how a crust can begin to form.
reason: I’ll check how the crystals can develop into the crustal rafts required by the remaining goal.

choice.inspect: Crystals in a cooling surface layer

expectation: A compatible partner will advance the solid layer toward floating crust.

effect: The crystals and surface melt formed fragile crustal rafts, completing the remaining goal.
reaction: It was satisfying to see cooling and crystallization produce a crust, with the reminder that it was temporary.

mostWorthwhile.text: Following metal droplets as they sank and merged made differentiation into a core and mantle understandable as a process rather than a prefabricated structure.

leastWorthwhile.text: The unsuccessful attempt to combine the magma ocean directly with gravity was the least productive, although its compatibility feedback helped identify the metal-droplet intermediate.

surprise.text: The first crust formed as fragile, temporary rafts that later impacts and upwelling could remake, rather than a permanent solid shell.

arbitrary.text: Combining the crystals with hot surface melt to make rafts was not obvious to me beforehand, though the result explained that the crystals gathered into solid patches.

continue.text: Yes. I would continue to see how the temporary crust and dissolved volatiles develop, since the chapter connected the combinations to clear physical processes.
